note: Offline emergency protocol cache — rendered when the network or the AI service is unavailable. Same provenance labels as the server corpus.

steps: Check responsiveness: tap the shoulders and shout. If no response and no normal breathing, treat as cardiac arrest.
Call for an ambulance (108/112) immediately, or send a specific bystander to call and fetch an AED if available.
Place the person on their back on a firm surface. Kneel beside their chest.
Position your hands: heel of one hand on the center of the chest, other hand on top, arms straight.
Give 30 chest compressions: push hard and fast, about 5-6 cm deep, at 100-120 per minute. Let the chest rise fully between pushes.
Give 2 rescue breaths only if trained: tilt the head, lift the chin, seal your mouth over theirs, blow for 1 second each.
Continue cycles of 30 compressions and 2 breaths until an AED arrives, professional help takes over, or the person starts breathing.
If an AED arrives, turn it on and follow the voice prompts. Apply pads to the bare chest and deliver a shock when instructed.
Resume CPR immediately after every shock.
Ask: 'Are you choking?' If the person cannot speak, cough, or breathe, act immediately.
Call for an ambulance (108/112) or have a bystander call.
Give 5 back blows: stand to the side and slightly behind, support the chest with one hand, lean the person forward, and strike firmly between the shoulder blades with the heel of your hand.
Give 5 abdominal thrusts (Heimlich): stand behind, make a fist above the navel, grasp it with the other hand, and pull sharply inward and upward.
Alternate 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts until the object clears or the person becomes unresponsive.
If the person becomes unresponsive, lower them to the floor and begin CPR, starting with compressions.
Call for an ambulance (108/112) for heavy bleeding that cannot be controlled quickly.
Wear gloves or use a plastic bag if available to protect yourself.
Expose the wound and apply firm, direct pressure with a sterile or clean cloth.
Do not remove soaked dressings; add new layers on top and keep pressing.
Elevate the injured limb above heart level if there is no suspected broken bone.
If bleeding continues through dressings, press on the pressure point above the wound and keep direct pressure on it.
Keep the person still, warm, and lying down; watch for pale, cold, clammy skin (shock) and reassure them until help arrives.
Stop the burning: remove the person from the heat source; smother flames with a blanket or water.
Cool the burn with cool running water for at least 10-20 minutes. Do not use ice or very cold water.
Remove jewellery and tight clothing near the burn before swelling starts, but do not peel off clothing stuck to the skin.
Cover the burn loosely with a clean, non-fluffy dressing or cling film laid lengthways.
Do not apply toothpaste, oil, butter, ointments, or ice to the burn.
Call an ambulance (108/112) for burns to the face, hands, feet, genitals, or any large or deep burn, and for any smoke inhalation or electrical burn.

procedures.source: Seed corpus — snakebite (India national protocol style)
steps: Move the person away from the snake and keep everyone calm and still. Do not try to catch or kill the snake.
Call for an ambulance (108/112) immediately — snakebite needs hospital assessment and possible anti-venom.
Keep the bitten limb still and lower than the heart. Remove rings, watches, and tight clothing from the limb.
Do NOT cut, suck, or apply tourniquet, ice, or herbs to the bite. Do not give the person anything to eat or drink.
Lay the person down and reassure them; panic increases the spread of venom.
If breathing stops, begin CPR. Monitor breathing and consciousness continuously until the ambulance arrives.
Stay calm and note the time the seizure started. Most seizures stop by themselves within 1-3 minutes.
Protect the person from injury: clear hard or sharp objects; place something soft under the head.
Do NOT restrain the person or put anything (spoon, fingers, cloth) in their mouth.
After shaking stops, roll the person onto their side (recovery position) to keep the airway clear.
Stay with them until fully alert and oriented. Call an ambulance (108/112) if the seizure lasts more than 5 minutes, repeats, or the person is injured, pregnant, or diabetic.
Check FAST: Face drooping on one side, Arm weakness or numbness, Speech difficulty, Time to call.
Call an ambulance (108/112) immediately — stroke treatment is time-critical. Note the exact time symptoms started.
Keep the person sitting or lying with head slightly raised. Do not give food, water, or medicines.
Loosen tight clothing and stay with the person, reassuring them.
If they become unresponsive and stop breathing normally, begin CPR.
Make the scene safe first: park safely behind the crash, hazard lights on, and put on a reflective vest if available.
Call 108/112 with the exact location, number of vehicles, and visible injuries.
Do not move casualties unless there is immediate danger (fire, traffic) — suspected spine injury makes movement risky.
Turn the engine off and warn oncoming traffic; do not smoke near spilled fuel.
Check responsive casualties: control bleeding with direct pressure, keep them warm and still.
Unresponsive but breathing: clear the airway and place on their side. Not breathing: begin CPR.
Stay until emergency services arrive and hand over what you observed.
Call the fire service (101) and evacuate immediately if the fire is spreading. Never fight a large fire yourself.
Alert everyone: shout, knock on doors, activate the nearest fire alarm.
Stay low under smoke — cleanest air is near the floor. Cover your nose and mouth with a cloth.
Touch doors with the back of your hand before opening; if hot, use another route.
Once out, stay out. Never go back inside for belongings.
If clothing catches fire: STOP, DROP, and ROLL to smother flames; cool burns with running water.
Meet at a pre-agreed assembly point and account for everyone.
Do NOT operate electrical switches, lights, phones, or any spark source inside the building — including turning anything off.
Evacuate everyone immediately, leaving doors and windows open if possible to ventilate.
Once outside and away from the leak, call the gas emergency line or 112.
Do not smoke or use lighters near the area; keep bystanders back.
If anyone feels dizzy, nauseous, or drowsy, move them to fresh air and call an ambulance (108).
Do not re-enter until the gas company or fire service declares it safe.
